title: Kejriwal Slams India's New Social Media Law Requiring Takedowns Within Three Hours
excerpt: The AAP leader accuses the Modi government of using tightened IT rules to silence critics, as police file a case against Meta's India head over Facebook videos targeting the PM.
body:
• Arvind Kejriwal has attacked India's amended IT rules requiring social media platforms to remove flagged content within three hours, down from 36
  • The AAP leader alleges the rules are designed to suppress criticism of PM Modi, calling them an attempt to 'crush the voice of Gen Z'
  • Police in Hyderabad have registered a case against Meta India head Arun Srinivas over Facebook videos depicting Modi in an 'abusive manner'
  • The tightened rules, effective since February 2026, have increased compliance pressure on global tech companies operating in India

Aam Aadmi Party leader Arvind Kejriwal has launched a sharp attack on India's tightened social media regulations, accusing the Modi government of using the amended IT rules to silence political opposition. The criticism comes as enforcement of the new rules intensifies, with police filing a case against Meta's India head over content posted on Facebook.

The Three-Hour Rule

India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules in February 2026, slashing the deadline for social media platforms to remove unlawful content from 36 hours to three hours after receiving a government or court order. Non-consensual intimate imagery must now be removed within two hours.

"Kejriwal alleged the rules are specifically designed to suppress dissent."

The amendments also impose stricter obligations around synthetically generated information, including AI-generated content and deepfakes, with platforms required to ensure proper labeling and provenance of such material, Reuters reported.

Kejriwal alleged the rules are specifically designed to suppress dissent. "Any post against PM Modi to be deleted in three hours," he said, urging the government to "do good work instead of crushing the voice of Gen Z." The ThePrint reported that Kejriwal described the rules as being "tightened to suppress people's voices."

Meta India Head Named in Police Case

The political stakes were underscored on July 31 when Hyderabad police registered a case against Meta India head Arun Srinivas over multiple Facebook videos depicting Modi in what officers described as an "abusive manner," Reuters reported. The videos spread as Modi contended with the largest wave of youth-led protests India has seen in more than a decade — a movement over leaked examination papers that led to the resignation of his education minister.

"We are in touch with the concerned agencies and are cooperating with them to resolve the matter."

— Meta spokesperson

It was not immediately clear why Srinivas was named personally, a rare move against a senior executive of a global tech firm. India's tightened content rules have narrowed the legal shield protecting platforms from liability for user-posted content, increasing the exposure of executives who run them.

Growing Tensions Over Online Speech

Government data shows the scale of content enforcement. Meta restricted more than 28,000 pieces of content in India in the first six months of 2025 alone following government requests, according to a Medium analysis. The Ministry of Home Affairs issued an average of 290 takedown notices per day in 2024-25, resulting in over 111,000 instances of blocked content.

The amendments have drawn criticism from digital rights organizations and opposition parties alike, who argue that the compressed timeline makes meaningful review of takedown requests impossible and effectively automates censorship. For global tech companies, India — their largest market by users — now presents one of the most demanding compliance environments in the world.
nri_angle: India's social media crackdown directly affects how the diaspora engages with Indian political discourse online, while the legal action against Meta's India head raises concerns about the regulatory environment for Indian-American tech executives.
author: Diaspora Desk
